prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR  
*What you’re seeing is **expected** behaviour in MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.11.*  
When a style **does not contain a `glyphs` URL**, MapLibre falls back to **“local‑fonts mode”**.  
Each entry in a layer’s `text‑font` array is treated exactly like a CSS `font‑family` list:

1. **If the font is already available on the device** (system font) → it is used.  
2. **If you have added a web‑font with `@font-face`** (or loaded it via `document.fonts.load`) → it is used.  
3. **If the name cannot be resolved** → the browser’s generic fallback (usually `sans‑serif`) is used, which is why you see a “generic” font.

No glyph‑PBFs are requested, no error is logged, and the map does **not** break. The only thing you lose is the guarantee that the map will look the same on every platform – the exact fallback font depends on the user’s OS and browser.

Below is a deeper dive into **what’s happening**, **why it isn’t a bug**, and **what you can do** if you need a deterministic font.

---

## 1. What “no `glyphs` property” really means

| Version | Behaviour when `glyphs` is missing |
|---------|-------------------------------------|
| **MapLibre GL JS < 5.11** | The style is considered invalid – the renderer will try to fetch glyph PBFs from a non‑existent URL, log an error, and the text may disappear. |
| **MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.11** | The style is **valid**. The engine switches to *local‑fonts mode* (see PR #4564). No network request for `/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` is made. The `text-font` array becomes a **cascading list of font‑family names** that the browser resolves exactly like CSS. |

> **Key point:** This fallback is **intentional** and documented. It is not a “bug” that the map still renders; it is a feature that lets you run completely offline or on a private intranet without a glyph server.

### 1.1. How the fallback works internally

1. **Parse `text-font`** – e.g. `["My Custom Font Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"]`.
2. **Iterate over the list** and ask the browser: *“Do you have a font with this exact family name?”*  
   - If you have added a web‑font with `@font-face` that declares `font-family: "My Custom Font Regular"`, the browser will use it.  
   - If not, the browser falls back to the next entry, eventually reaching the generic system font.
3. **Render each glyph with TinySDF** – a tiny signed‑distance‑field generator that runs in the main thread. This is the same code path that is used when a glyph PBF fails to load, only it is applied to **every** code‑point because there is no PBF source.

Because TinySDF works on the **actual font file** the browser selected, the visual quality is still good (SDF scaling, crisp at any zoom), but the *shape* of the letters is whatever the local font provides.

---

## 2. Why you see a “generic” font

* The font name you wrote in `text-font` **does not match any loaded font** on the client.
* Common reasons:
  - You never loaded the font at all (no `<link>` or `@font-face`).
  - The `font-family` name in the CSS does **not** exactly match the string in `text-font` (case‑sensitive, spaces matter).
  - The font is a system font that simply isn’t installed on the user’s OS (e.g., “Roboto” on a Windows machine without the font).

When none of the names resolve, the browser falls back to its default generic family (`sans-serif` on most platforms), which is why you see a “generic” look.

---

## 3. What you can do

### 3.1. Keep the current “local‑fonts” approach (recommended for offline / private deployments)

1. **Load the font yourself** (web‑font or system‑installed) **before** the map is created.  
   ```html
   <!-- Example using a self‑hosted WOFF2 -->
   <style>
     @font-face {
       font-family: "My Custom Font Regular";
       src: url("/fonts/MyCustomFont-Regular.woff2") format("woff2");
       font-weight: normal;
       font-style: normal;
     }
   </style>
   ```
   Or, if you prefer a CDN:
   ```html
   <link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Roboto:wght@400&display=swap"
         rel="stylesheet">
   <style>
     @font-face {
       font-family: "Roboto";
       src: local('Roboto'), url('https://fonts.gstatic.com/s/roboto/v30/KFOmCnqEu92Fr1Mu4mxM.woff2') format('woff2');
     }
   </style>
   ```

2. **Make sure the `font-family` name matches exactly** the string you put in `text-font`.  
   ```json
   {
     "type": "symbol",
     "layout": {
       "text-field": "{name}",
       "text-font": ["My Custom Font Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"]
     }
   }
   ```

3. **Optional – wait for the font to be ready** before creating the map (helps avoid a flash of the generic fallback):
   ```js
   document.fonts.ready.then(() => {
     const map = new maplibregl.Map({ /* … */ });
   });
   ```

4. **CJK / Ideographs** – If you also need Chinese/Japanese/Korean characters, you can keep the default `localIdeographFontFamily` (which uses the OS’s built‑in CJK rasterizer) or set it to a specific on‑device font:
   ```js
   const map = new maplibregl.Map({
     container: 'map',
     style: 'style.json',
     localIdeographFontFamily: '"Noto Sans CJK SC", sans-serif' // optional
   });
   ```

> **Result:** The map will render with the exact font you supplied, offline, without any glyph server.

### 3.2. Switch to a classic glyph‑PBF workflow (useful when you need pixel‑perfect cross‑platform rendering)

1. **Add a `glyphs` URL** to your style JSON, pointing at a server that serves the `{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` tree.  
   ```json
   {
     "glyphs": "https://my.cdn.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
     ...
   }
   ```

2. **Provide the matching PBFs** for every font you reference in `text-font`.  
   - For common fonts (Noto, Open Sans, Roboto, etc.) you can copy the pre‑built trees from the **openmaptiles/fonts** or **UNDP‑Data/fonts** repositories.  
   - For a brand‑new font, generate the PBFs with **Font Maker** (`npm i -g @mapbox/font-maker`) or **fontnik**.

3. **Deploy a tiny static server** (e.g., Nginx, Cloudflare Workers, or even GitHub Pages) that serves the `.pbf` files with the correct MIME type (`application/x-protobuf`).

4. **Keep `text-font` unchanged** – the names must match the folder names on the server.

> **Result:** All clients (GL JS, MapLibre Native, mobile SDKs) will fetch the same pre‑computed glyphs, guaranteeing identical visual output across browsers, OSes, and devices.

### 3.3. When you *must* support MapLibre Native **and** GL JS with the same style

- **Do NOT rely on the omit‑`glyphs` fallback** – Native currently has no equivalent and will simply show nothing for any text.
- **Provide a `glyphs` URL** and the corresponding PBFs **or** use the **`font-faces`** property (Native‑only) to map `text-font` names to local font files.  
  - `font-faces` is a separate array in the style (Android ≥ 11.13, iOS ≥ 6.18) and is **ignored by GL JS**.  
  - Keep both sections in the same style if you need a hybrid solution, but remember they are independent.

---

## 4. Quick checklist – “Is my map doing what I expect?”

| ✅ | Check |
|---|-------|
| **1** | `glyphs` is **absent** in the style → you are in local‑fonts mode. |
| **2** | The font name in `text-font` exactly matches a `font-family` you have loaded (via `@font-face` or a system font). |
| **3** | `document.fonts.ready` resolves **before** you create the map (optional, avoids flash). |
| **4** | For CJK characters, either keep the default `localIdeographFontFamily` or set it to a specific on‑device CJK font. |
| **5** | If you need deterministic cross‑platform rendering, add a `glyphs` URL and serve the matching PBFs. |
| **6** | If you also target MapLibre Native, do **not** rely on the omit‑`glyphs` fallback; provide a glyph server or `font-faces`. |

If all of the above are true, the behaviour you see is **exactly what the library is designed to do**.

---

## 5. Common pitfalls & how to avoid them

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| Text appears in *different* fonts on Chrome vs. Firefox | Font name mismatch or missing `@font-face` → each browser falls back to its own system default. | Verify the `font-family` string, load the font early, and optionally use `document.fonts.ready`. |
| Text disappears after a style reload | `glyphs` was added back to the style but the server returns 404 for the requested range. | Either keep `glyphs` omitted, or ensure the server hosts the full `{fontstack}/{range}.pbf` tree. |
| CJK characters look blocky or missing | `localIdeographFontFamily` set to `false` (or not set) and the glyph server does not provide CJK PBFs. | Remove the `false` setting, or serve CJK glyphs (large, many requests). |
| Arabic/Hebrew letters are reversed or missing diacritics | RTL plugin not loaded, or script‑specific shaping not supported. | Load the RTL plugin (`setRTLTextPlugin`) **before** map creation. |
| Devanagari text shows each code‑point as a separate box | No shaping engine; MapLibre cannot render complex ligatures. | Currently there is no fix – you must accept the limitation or use raster images for those labels. |

Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** for getting **offline, local‑font rendering** to work with **MapLibre Native on Android**.  
It assumes you are using a recent native SDK (Android ≥ 11.13.0, iOS ≥ 6.18.0) because the `font‑faces` property was added in those releases.

---

## 1. Why `glyphs` → local fallback does **not** work in Native

| Platform | What happens when `glyphs` is omitted or a PBF fails |
|----------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **MapLibre GL JS (≥ 5.11.0)** | Falls back to **TinySDF** and renders the text with any web/system font you have loaded. |
| **MapLibre Native** | **No fallback** – the style **must** contain a `glyphs` URL **or** a `font‑faces` block. If `glyphs` is missing, the map will simply show no text (or a “missing glyph” placeholder). |

So the only way to go “offline‑only” on Android is to **declare local font files** with the `font‑faces` property.

---

## 2. High‑level workflow

1. **Pick the fonts you want to use** (e.g. Noto Sans, Noto Sans Arabic, Noto Sans Devanagari, a brand font, etc.).  
2. **Copy the font files (TTF/OTF) into your Android app’s assets** (or `res/raw`).  
3. **Create a `font‑faces` array** in the style JSON that maps each `text‑font` name to one or more local font files **and** the Unicode ranges those files cover.  
4. **Reference those names in every layer’s `text‑font`** (fallback list works the same as with glyph PBFs).  
5. **Bundle the style JSON with the app** (or download it once and cache it). No external `glyphs` endpoint is needed.  

---

## 3. Preparing the font files

| What you need | Where to get it | Tips |
|---------------|----------------|------|
| **Noto Sans (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic)** | <https://github.com/googlefonts/noto-fonts/tree/main/hinted/ttf/NotoSans> | Use the *Regular* weight for the base style; add *Bold* / *Italic* if you need them. |
| **Noto Sans Arabic** | <https://github.com/googlefonts/noto-fonts/tree/main/hinted/ttf/NotoSansArabic> | Arabic needs RTL shaping – Native already runs the `maplibre-gl-rtl-text` plugin internally, you just need the font. |
| **Noto Sans Devanagari** | <https://github.com/googlefonts/noto-fonts/tree/main/hinted/ttf/NotoSansDevanagari> | Remember Devanagari shaping is **not** supported – you’ll get a “box‑y” look. See the limitation note below. |
| **Custom brand font** | Your own .ttf/.otf | Make sure the file is **not** compressed (keep the original). |

**Copy the files** into `app/src/main/assets/fonts/` (or `res/raw/`).  
If you use the assets folder, the path you will reference later is `fonts/<file>.ttf`.

---

## 4. Building the `font‑faces` block

The `font‑faces` property lives **inside the top‑level style object**, alongside `sources`, `layers`, etc.

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "none",                     // <-- can be any placeholder; it will be ignored
  "font-faces": [
    {
      "font-family": "Noto Sans Regular",
      "src": [
        {
          "url": "asset://fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf",
          "format": "truetype"
        }
      ],
      "unicode-range": "U+0000-00FF, U+0100-024F, U+0250-02AF, U+1E00-1EFF"
    },
    {
      "font-family": "Noto Sans Bold",
      "src": [
        {
          "url": "asset://fonts/NotoSans-Bold.ttf",
          "format": "truetype"
        }
      ],
      "unicode-range": "U+0000-00FF, U+0100-024F, U+0250-02AF, U+1E00-1EFF"
    },
    {
      "font-family": "Noto Sans Arabic Regular",
      "src": [
        {
          "url": "asset://fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf",
          "format": "truetype"
        }
      ],
      "unicode-range": "U+0600-06FF, U+0750-077F, U+08A0-08FF, U+FB50-FDFF, U+FE70-FEFF"
    },
    {
      "font-family": "Noto Sans CJK SC Regular",
      "src": [
        {
          "url": "asset://fonts/NotoSansSC-Regular.otf",
          "format": "opentype"
        }
      ],
      "unicode-range": "U+4E00-9FFF, U+3400-4DBF, U+20000-2A6DF, U+2A700-2B73F, U+2B740-2B81F"
    }
    // …add more script blocks as needed
  ],
  "sources": { … },
  "layers":  [ … ]
}
```

### Important fields

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `font-family` | The **exact string** you will later use in `text-font`. It can contain spaces, but keep it identical everywhere. |
| `src` → `url` | `asset://` tells the native SDK to load the file from the **app’s assets**. If you placed the file in `res/raw`, use `raw://<resource_name>` instead. |
| `src` → `format` | Either `"truetype"` (`.ttf`) or `"opentype"` (`.otf`). |
| `unicode-range` | **Comma‑separated list** of Unicode ranges that this file covers. The SDK will only use the file for code points inside those ranges. If you omit the property, the file is considered to cover **all** code points (expensive, not recommended). |
| `glyphs` | Can be any placeholder (`"none"` or a dummy URL). It is ignored when `font-faces` is present. |

> **Tip:** Keep the `unicode-range` as tight as possible. It lets the renderer skip loading a font file for a tile that does not need it, which is crucial for performance on low‑end devices.

---

## 5. Using the fonts in layer definitions

Now you can reference the fonts exactly as you would with a glyph‑PBF stack:

```json
{
  "id": "road-labels",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "openmaptiles",
  "source-layer": "transportation_name",
  "layout": {
    "text-field": ["get", "name"],
    "text-font": [
      "Noto Sans Bold",               // primary (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic)
      "Noto Sans Arabic Regular",    // fallback for Arabic
      "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular" // fallback for Devanagari (will look wrong – see limitation)
    ],
    "text-size": 12,
    "text-anchor": "center"
  },
  "paint": {
    "text-color": "#222"
  }
}
```

*The order matters*: the first font that **covers the code point** (according to its `unicode-range`) will be used. If none match, the text is omitted.

---

## 6. Wiring it up in Android code

```kotlin
// 1️⃣ Load the style JSON from assets (or from a cached file)
val styleJson = assets.open("style/offline-style.json")
    .bufferedReader()
    .use { it.readText() }

// 2️⃣ Create the map
val map = MapLibreMap(
    context = this,
    mapOptions = MapOptions(
        // optional: set a custom cache directory, etc.
    )
)

// 3️⃣ Set the style (the SDK parses `font-faces` automatically)
map.setStyle(
    style = styleJson,
    // you can also pass a URL if you download the style once and cache it
)

// 4️⃣ (Optional) If you want to change the default font‑family for CJK ideographs,
//    you can set `localIdeographFontFamily` – but note that Native does **not**
//    have the GL‑JS “local‑ideograph” shortcut. You must provide a CJK font
//    via `font-faces` as shown above.
```

That’s it – the map will now render all labels using the **bundled fonts**, without ever contacting a glyph server.

---

## 7. Special cases & gotchas

| Issue | What to do |
|-------|------------|
| **CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) characters** | Native **does not** have the GL‑JS `localIdeographFontFamily` shortcut. If you want fast offline rendering, **include a CJK font** (e.g. `Noto Sans CJK SC`) in `font-faces` and list it in `text-font`. The Unicode range for CJK is huge, so keep the font file size reasonable (use the *SC* or *TC* subset you need). |
| **Arabic / Hebrew** | The SDK already ships the `maplibre-gl-rtl-text` plugin internally, so you only need the appropriate font in `font-faces`. No extra code required. |
| **Devanagari, Khmer, Bengali, etc.** | **Shaping is not supported** in MapLibre Native (same limitation as GL‑JS). | **Weight & style (Bold, Italic)** | Treat each weight as a separate `font-family` entry (e.g., `"Noto Sans Bold"`). The `unicode-range` can be identical to the regular weight; the renderer will pick the first matching entry in the `text-font` list. |

| **CORS / asset URLs** | When you load the style from a remote URL (even if you later cache it), the `src` URLs inside `font-faces` **must** be `asset://` or `raw://`. Remote URLs are not allowed for offline‑only fonts. |
| **Testing** | Turn on `MapLibreMapOptions.debug = true` (or `map.setDebug(true)`) to see console logs like `Loading font Noto Sans Bold from asset://fonts/NotoSans-Bold.ttf`. If a code point is missing you’ll see `No matching font‑face for U+0E01`. |
| **Version compatibility** | `font-faces` was introduced in **Android SDK 11.13.0** (released 2024‑09). If you are on an older version you must either upgrade or fall back to a glyph‑PBF server. |

---
